title: Instrumented Handle for Stroke Rehab
outcome: 3 PCB spins → 115 × 33 mm, <80 g instrumented utensil handle
tldr: Utensil-sized rehab handle sensing 0–100 N grip force, tremor, and orientation — three PCB spins from a bulky 2-layer board to a slim edge-mount board with strain relief and test pads.
role: Research contributor — electronics & mechanical integration lead (3 PCB spins, Utah NeuroRobotics Lab)
problem: Rehab trials needed a utensil-sized handle (115 mm × 33 mm, <80 g) that senses grip force, stab force, tremor, and orientation in real time without the wiring harness failing under strain.
process: PCB #1: packed 2-layer board (IMU, Hall, load cells, ADCs, BLE) — bulky, harness failures
PCB #2: stacked layout, dedicated connector block, cleaner analog front-end routing
PCB #3: slim edge-mount board inside the handle body, strain relief, breakout test pads
build: Paired load cells in finger channel, 2-axis thumb force element, in-line 3-axis accelerometer, Hall + two-magnet orientation. Sensor leads routed through a 3D-printed internal spine, hand-soldered, bench-tested, then potted and enclosed.
learned: Analog routing and strain relief decide whether a wearable survives real-world clinical handling; test pads pay for themselves in trial debug time.

title: Soft Supernumerary Robotic Limb
outcome: CSEF Saban 1st ($1,500); 2.2 cm point error, 92.4 lb peak payload
tldr: Wearable 9-segment Ecoflex 00-30 silicone continuum arm with 12-stepper tendon drive and Discrete Cosserat Rod control — $247 BOM, 16.1 lb system, 2.2 cm avg point error across 8 trials, 92.4 lb max tested payload.
role: Solo developer — silicone molding, 12-motor tendon drive, Cosserat control
problem: Extend human reach and load capacity with a low-cost, compliant wearable extra limb that moves smoothly around the torso without rigid exoskeleton bulk.
process: Iterated from spine-vertebrae and origami-wing prototypes to 9-segment Ecoflex 00-30 silicone modules cast over fiber-reinforced actuators (FRAs) and rigid endcaps
Built 12-stepper (360°, 4 tendons × 3 modules) tendon drive on a 3D-printed PLA backplate + nylon torso harness
Implemented Discrete Cosserat Rod path planning with vision + speech intention control; validated across 45 randomized target points and 8-trial error tracking
build: Torso-mounted 9-segment silicone continuum arm driven by 12 stepper motors, Raspberry Pi controller, and 48 AA battery pack ($247 total materials).

testing.value: 16.1 lb ($247 BOM); 92.4 lb max @ 157 N tension

learned: Elastomer continuum segments paired with Discrete Cosserat Rod kinematics deliver repeatable 3D reachability without rigid-link pinch hazards.

title: Wireless taVNS Biostimulant Earbud
outcome: Working prototype <$200; Al electrodes 0.9 Ω vs 165 kΩ composite
tldr: Wireless earbud pairing BLE audio with biphasic taVNS stimulation for motion sickness — KiCad PCB, Phrozen 16K resin housing, machined aluminum electrodes (0.9 Ω vs 165.0 kΩ graphite-silicone, n=6), under $200 BOM.
role: Co-developer (3-student FSRI team; Gao Research Group, Caltech) — KiCad PCB, housing, electrodes
problem: Commercial and experimental taVNS devices are bulky, wired, and cannot simultaneously stream audio. Motion-sickness relief needed a self-contained wireless earbud targeting the concha and cymba concha.
process: DigiKey component selection + datasheet verification; breadboard circuit validation
KiCad schematic + layout: USB-C charger, 3.3 V buck/boost, 32 V boost rail, IDAC, quad-switch (biphasic), BLE audio amp
Iterated Phrozen 16K resin housings to fix thin-wall/connector retention; pivoted from cast graphite-silicone electrodes to machined aluminum after 6-trial multimeter comparison
build: 0–5 mA controllable biphasic constant-current stimulation with fail-safes; BLE audio streaming; SLA resin enclosure with machined aluminum concha/cymba-concha electrodes.
learned: Electrode contact impedance dominated system feasibility — quantitative n=6 resistance testing forced an early pivot off composite silicone.

title: Drone Belly Mount for Hyperspectral Camera
outcome: 2 CAD/FEA iterations; 1.59 MPa max stress at 20 N for 1.5 kg camera
tldr: Belly mount hanging a 1.5 kg MicroHSI 410 hyperspectral camera from a DJI Matrice-class drone — two print iterations, SolidWorks FEA at 20 N (1.59 MPa max stress, 0.015 mm displacement), bench-fitted on drone.
role: CAD, FEA & 3D-print lead — SJSU ARAS Lab (autonomous remote sensing team)
problem: Mount a ~1.5 kg (14.7 N) MicroHSI 410 hyperspectral camera straight-down (no gimbal) onto the DJI Matrice's damped belly plate without blocking heat sinks, ports, or markings or shifting CG off-axis.
process: CADed an L-bracket cradle and base plate in SolidWorks around exact camera envelope, adding draft, fillets, relief cuts, and heat-set inserts
Iter 1 (PLA/PETG): physical fit check exposed rear screw-boss interference + lug hole misalignment → shortened body ~1/8 in, added camera pocket, reprinted at 20% gyroid
Iter 2: thickened mounting tabs and base plate, switched to ribbing over infill, and ran SolidWorks linear static FEA (ABS, 20 N load) on both plate and cradle
build: Two-part printed cradle and base plate with heat-set inserts; bolt-pattern, port-clearance, and CG verified physically on the DJI Matrice airframe.

testing.value: ~1.5 kg (14.7 N static) tested at 20 N
1.59 MPa plate / 1.24 MPa cradle, 0.015 mm disp.
Bench-fitted on DJI body; >30 N pull & flight tests next

learned: Isotropic linear FEA misses infill geometry and layer-to-layer anisotropy — physical >30 N load testing is required before flight sign-off.

title: VEX Drivetrain Testing + Bézier Autonomy
outcome: 6-motor mecanum selected from 3 testbeds; field-centric odometry planner
tldr: Built three identical drivable testbeds (tank vs X-drive vs 6-motor mecanum) to compare sprint speed and current-logged push force, picked mecanum, then drove it with a C++ odometry + Bézier planner.
problem: Pick a drivetrain base that balances cycle speed and scrum pushing force, then execute simultaneous translate-and-rotate autonomous routines without stop-turn-drive penalties.
process: Built three full-width testbeds: 6-wheel tank, X-drive, 6-motor mecanum (same brain/IMU placement for equal weight distribution)
Timed straight-line sprints under load and ran barrier-push tests with motor current logging to compare usable stall force
Integrated X/Y tracking wheels → continuous X/Y/θ pose → Bézier-curve planner with rolling lookahead; tuned in jerry.io sim before real-robot drift correction
build: 6-motor mecanum chassis with 45° roller geometry and traction tuning; orthogonal X/Y odometry wheel stack; C++ field-centric waypoint routines around stakes, rings, and drop-off.
learned: Controlled A/B testbeds settle drivetrain debates fast; sim-first Bézier path tuning reduced on-field autonomous debugging.

title: Reclaiming 7th Street: Reconfigurable Housing Prototype
outcome: Autodesk Make It Home Grand Prize (Best Physical Prototype); Bambu X1E model
tldr: Modular West Oakland housing development drafted in AutoCAD, modeled in Fusion 360, and 3D-printed in PLA on a Bambu Lab X1E as an interlocking scale model — won Autodesk's Grand Prize for Best Physical Prototype.
role: Solo designer & builder — AutoCAD floor plans, Fusion 360 assembly, 3D-printed prototype
problem: Reimagine an underinvested West Oakland corridor into reconfigurable, community-owned housing with commercial ground floors and prove modular assembly logic physically.
process: Drafted commercial, communal, and swappable apartment-cube floor plans in AutoCAD tailored to West Oakland's 7th Street site and transit bridge
Modeled multi-story structural supports, vertical gardens, greywater loops, and under-bridge VAWTs in Fusion 360
Sliced modular unit batches in Bambu Studio and printed PLA prototypes on a Bambu Lab X1E (218 °C nozzle / 55 °C bed); tuned mating tolerances with flush cutters, 320-grit sanding, and needle files
build: Multi-level 3D-printed PLA scale model with removable/reconfigurable residential cubes, commercial podium, cyanoacrylate/two-part epoxy joints, and vertical-garden foliage.

testing.value: Bambu Lab X1E (PLA), needle-file joint fit check

learned: Printing individual modular cubes forced crisp mating clearances early — physical fit checks caught joint tolerances that CAD renders hide.

title: Pit Cooling Rig + Box Bot
outcome: 4-fan cooling PCB + powered cart moving 30+ lb robot
tldr: Pit-side reliability hardware: a 4-fan high-static-pressure cooling rig with custom fan-control PCB plus a modular 3D-printed powered cart that hauls the 30+ lb competition robot.
role: Designer & builder — pit cooling rig, fan-control PCB & powered cart (Bobaionics 12478X)
problem: Drivetrain motors overheated between back-to-back tournament matches, and hauling a 30+ lb competition robot across large venues risked frame damage and drops.
process: Modeled airflow for 4 high-static-pressure PC fans in a custom VEX frame; routed housing panels and laid out a dedicated fan-control schematic and PCB
CADed and 3D-printed a modular box-bot cart with integrated wiring channels, DeWalt battery bay, controller mount, removable access panels, and quick-grab handles
build: Custom fan-control PCB powering 4 high-static-pressure pit fans under a drop-on robot deck; multi-part 3D-printed cart chassis with impact brackets and cable strain relief.
learned: Pit infrastructure is a force multiplier — active between-match cooling and rugged transport directly protect match consistency.
